title: The corridor (Avot 4:16)
hookLine: the backstage hallway before the curtain: this world is like a corridor before the banquet hall; prepare in the corridor
tomorrow: if this is just the hallway, does any hour here count?

lines: WHAT DO YOU DO IN THE HALLWAY?
cards: The hallway before the curtain smells like hairspray and dust and somebody's orange. The lights are low. Through the wall, the murmur of a full house, a cough, a program dropped.

Everyone back here is doing something small: checking a prop, fixing a collar, mouthing a first line. What do you do in the hallway before the curtain? A sage in Avot says that's the question of a whole life.

teach.b: Rabbi Yaakov says it in two lines. This world is like a corridor before the world to come. Prepare yourself in the corridor, so that you may enter the banquet hall.
The Hebrew words are a picture.
The corridor is the prozdor, the entrance passage. The banquet hall is the traklin, the great dining room, where the feast is laid.
In Rabbi Yaakov's picture, you don't live in the hallway forever, and you don't skip it either. You get ready in it.
So what does getting ready look like? Here's what's surprising: it's small. A collar straightened.
A line said once more. A prop put where your hand will find it in the dark. Nobody in the audience will ever see the corridor, and every good moment on stage was made there.
Jewish teaching holds a range of views about what the world to come is like, and this saying doesn't describe it.

It describes the hallway, and what to do in it. One caution: some people hear corridor and think this world doesn't matter, it's just a passage. Avot's very next saying will push hard on that reading.
For today, the job is simple.

how: Many Jews prepare for Shabbat in the hours before it begins, cooking, cleaning and setting the table, and the tradition often reads that weekly getting-ready as a picture of preparing in this world.

o: this world, as the hallway where you get ready
the line of people waiting to be judged after death
a long hall in the Temple where priests waited

games.q: the corridor and the hall — tap the pairs.

s: the corridor saying means this world doesn't matter
it says prepare in the corridor, and Avot's next saying pushes hard on that reading.
the saying describes in detail what the world to come is like
it describes the hallway and what to do in it; Jewish views of the world to come vary.
traklin is the banquet hall in Rabbi Yaakov's picture
the corridor, prozdor, leads into the traklin.

games.q: you have a big interview next week. it's three days away and nothing about it feels real yet. what fits Rabbi Yaakov's corridor?
o: do one small thing today: print the directions, lay out what you'll wear.
wait until the night before; the corridor is just a hallway to rush through.
skip preparing; what happens in the room is all that really counts.
games.why: prepare in the corridor. the getting ready is small and unseen, and it's where the moment in the hall is made.

practice: Get one small thing ready for tomorrow, right now: your keys by the door, a glass of water by the bed, the shoes you'll wear. Hold it a moment, feel its weight and texture, and set it exactly where your hand will find it.
Then sit back down for the rest of the sit, in your own corridor.

wordCard.voice: The corridor. Rabbi Yaakov: this world is like a corridor before the world to come; prepare yourself there, for the banquet hall.

orig.note: Hebrew in the Mishnah: a corridor or entrance passage, the hallway before the hall.

carryVoice: Pocket this: prepare in the corridor, where nobody sees and everything is made. Forty of sixty: places, please.

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 4:16 (Rabbi Yaakov: this world is like a corridor before the world to come)
